chapter: Billy Pierce Studio and New York tap
title: Tap dancing in the Depression
summary: Green and his co-interviewer say tap was cheerful stuff that helped people forget the crash, with work plentiful on Broadway.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: You must remember now, in those times America was overcoming the stock market crash. See? They was trying to -- they was in the process of overcoming that.

Yeah. The Depression. So I mean, every- thing was still -- they was trying to be as lucrative, or plentiful as possible, and they was trying to sell everything, you see? You see what I mean. Tap dancing was tap dancing, right on, you see, because --

Most of At the studios they would always have tap included. They would have tap and they would say whatever other kind of dancing, you know. But there would be tap first. The work was plentiful in show business then because people -- they wanted the people to forget about the Depression, not to take it too hard, you see? And they was trying to get people's minds off of these great losses that occurred in the crash,

you know, the stock market crash in 1929, see, and so Broadway was actually a Mecca, especially around that part of the city, which was in like 40 -- well, you must go from Columbus Circle all the way down to 14th Street, the theatrical part. Shubert's Alley, Tin Pan Alley, and so on, you know. It was very lucrative, especially entertainment, the entertainment world.
So tap dancing really was a form of making people -- a dance form that was geared toward making people forget where they came from, bringing them into something different, making them happy.
